catalog_quote: The metrical system is trochaic, that is, feet are left-headed. These trochaic feet are created from left to right (i.e. from the beginning to the end of words). Generally, metrical feet in Kashibo-Kakataibo have to be disyllabic and degenerate feet are only admitted under very specific circumstances (see §4.3.6). In addition, the position of the primary stress (manifested as vowel lengthening) follows a different principle for predicates and non-predicates. Predicates carry the primary stress on the head of the rightmost (i.e. last) foot. Non-predicates carry the primary stress on the head of the leftmost (i.e. first) foot. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (realised as vowel lengthening, not pitch) is metrical and weight-insensitive: disyllabic trochees are built from the left edge and no degenerate feet are formed. Non-predicates (nouns and other words in citation/argument use) carry primary stress on the first syllable, the head of the leftmost foot. Predicates carry primary stress on the head of the rightmost complete foot, i.e. the penult in even-numbered and the antepenult in odd-numbered syllable counts (e.g. (pi.a)(KË.xa) 'ate long ago'). A high tone, treated as a separate feature, goes on the rightmost prominent syllable (the stressed syllable or a closed syllable in even position to its right); a word's final syllable cannot carry it unless lexically marked. Alternative catalog reading: tone language with a stress statement, since the author describes a system combining stress and (non-obligatory) high tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Heads of non-primary feet carry secondary stress, realised as a vowel longer than in non-prominent syllables (§4.3.3, p. 135-136: (»ba.ka)(«ka.ma) 'river=PLU', («pi.a)(»kë.xa)). Trisyllables form one foot only; the third syllable takes no secondary stress and stays short (p. 133).
new_statements.exceptions: A separate high tone (non-obligatory, non-culminative, weight-sensitive, partly lexical) regularly falls elsewhere than the stress: disyllables with a final consonant (overt or underlying) have stress on syllable 1 but high tone on syllable 2 (§4.3.1.2-3, pp. 128-131); some monomorphemic tri-/tetrasyllabic words have a lexical high tone on syllable 2 while stress stays on syllable 1; a few suffixes (e.g. -ín 'proximal') carry lexical high tone without stress (§4.3.9); monosyllables surface with extra-long vowels to satisfy the minimal-word requirement (§4.3.5); Shell (1950, 1987) had analysed the high pitch as stress. Author calls the account preliminary (p. 121).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word: stress is obligatory and culminative per phonological word (definition (150), p. 167: a unit of at least two syllables/one foot and one stress); each word in an NP has its own primary stress; grammatical words of five or more syllables may split into two prosodic units each with a primary stress; adverbial enclitics may carry their own stress. 'Predicate' vs 'non-predicate' is a syntactic-function split, not noun vs verb (fn. 28, p. 124): most words can be predicates and are then prosodically treated as such; nominalised verbs count as non-predicates. Data are instrumentally measured (Praat) elicited words and sentences from two adult male speakers of the Lower Aguaytía dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted description is of the Lower Aguaytía dialect of Kashibo-Kakataibo (Zariquiey 2011, Tables 12-13 and p. 74), the same language-level languoid cash1251 [cbr]; author names the language Kashibo-Kakataibo (2011) / Kakataibo (2018). Older sources call it Cashibo.

readall_conflicts: Neither listed work could be read, so no new source-to-source disagreement was found. One point of tension already inside the record: the catalog entry initial stress (initial stress) and the existing statement's 'fixed: initial syllable' summarise only half of Zariquiey 2011's rule. The same grammar (already held by the project, PDF p. 155 = thesis p. 124, and PDF p. 167 = §4.3.6) says: 'Predicates carry the primary stress on the head of the rightmost (i.e. last) foot. Non-predicates carry the primary stress on the head of the leftmost (i.e. first) foot.' — so initial stress holds for nouns and other non-predicates, while verbs (predicates) stress the head of the last trochaic foot; and a separate, weight-sensitive high tone is placed on the rightmost prominent syllable. The catalog reading is therefore correct for non-predicates but the record should note the predicate/non-predicate split and the tone overlay.
